title: The occasion (summer 1797)
short: Written at Nether Stowey in summer 1797, when an accident kept Coleridge at home while his visitors went walking on the Quantock hills.
body: Coleridge's headnote says that 'long-expected friends' arrived in June 1797 and that an accident on the morning of their arrival disabled him from walking. A letter to Southey of July 1797 is more specific: his wife Sara had spilt a skillet of boiling milk on his foot. The friends were Charles Lamb, down from London, and William and Dorothy Wordsworth, who were about to settle at Alfoxden a few miles away. Left behind, Coleridge composed the poem in a garden bower beside his cottage. A shorter draft went to Southey (the letter is now in the Morgan Library) and another to Charles Lloyd. The poem was first printed in Southey's Annual Anthology (1800) and revised for Sibylline Leaves (1817). The opening 'Well,' sets the casual, spoken tone of the 'conversation poems'.

title: lime-tree bower ... prison
short: The lime is the linden tree (Tilia), not the citrus; a pleasant arbour is ironically called a prison.
body: The lime-tree here is the linden, a common English shade tree. A 'bower' is a garden arbour, a place of retreat in pastoral and romance; to call it a 'prison' is half-humorous self-pity, and the poem's whole movement undoes the paradox. By line 48 the same place is 'This little lime-tree bower', in which he has 'marked / Much that has soothed me'. Physical confinement becomes imaginative freedom: he follows the walkers in his mind, and then finds that the narrow plot itself repays attention. The Annual Anthology title added 'A Poem Addressed to Charles Lamb, of the India House, London'; the words were dropped in later editions.

title: springy
short: Coleridge glossed his own adjective in the manuscript letter to Southey: 'Elastic, I mean.'
body: In the manuscript letter to Southey Coleridge added the gloss 'Elastic, I mean': the heath gives under the walker's foot and springs back. The OED records 'springy' in this sense of elastic or resilient. The detail is imagined, not seen. Coleridge projects into the walkers' bodies a sensation he cannot share, which is the method of the poem's first movement (ll. 1-20), a guided tour conducted in absence. Note also 'Friends, whom I never more may meet again' (l. 6), a melodramatic touch that the poem's growing cheerfulness quietly corrects.

title: the roaring dell
short: A narrow wooded ravine with a waterfall in the Quantocks, which Coleridge had told his friends about; 'still' means 'continually'.
body: 'Of which I told' shows that Coleridge had described the place to his guests beforehand. 'Still' carries the older sense 'always, continually' (OED), so the dell is never silent; the next line repeats 'The roaring dell' as if savouring it. The adjectives 'o'erwooded, narrow, deep' and 'only speckled by the mid-day sun' make it a place of near darkness, which the poem contrasts with the open 'wide wide Heaven' of line 22. In the letter to Southey the dell was 'rifted' and many an ash 'Twists its wild limbs beside the ferny rock'; revision concentrates the scene into the single branchless ash.

title: the branchless ash
short: An ash flung across the ravine like a bridge, its few leaves stirred not by wind but by the draught of the waterfall.
body: The leaves 'Ne'er tremble in the gale, yet tremble still, / Fanned by the water-fall': a small paradox, since sheltered from the wind they move all the same. Readers have taken the tree as an emblem of the poet himself, cut off from the breezes the others enjoy yet still moved by a hidden source, and it anticipates the closing claim that no plot is so narrow that Nature is absent. Moving air as a figure for inspiration runs through Coleridge's poetry, from 'The Eolian Harp' to 'Dejection'; Abrams traced the pattern in his essay on the 'correspondent breeze'.

title: long lank weeds
short: Coleridge identified these 'weeds' in a footnote as the hart's-tongue fern, Asplenium scolopendrium.
body: Coleridge's footnote names the plant as Asplenium scolopendrium, 'called in some countries the Adder's Tongue, in others the Hart's Tongue', adding that William Withering's botany reserves 'Adder's Tongue' for Ophioglossum. The fern's long strap-shaped fronds hang from the wet rock; the 'fantastic sight' is that they all nod and drip together 'beneath the dripping edge / Of the blue clay-stone' (the 1800 text had 'dim'). The care for correct naming shows how seriously Coleridge took exact natural observation.

title: the wide wide Heaven
short: The doubled adjective marks the walkers' emergence from the dark dell into open sky; it echoes 'Alone on a wide wide sea' in the Ancient Mariner.
body: The second verse paragraph opens with release: from the enclosed dell the friends climb out to a panoramic view of 'hilly fields and meadows, and the sea'. Doubling 'wide' imitates the sense of expansion. The same unusual repetition occurs in The Rime of the Ancyent Marinere, written in the same months and printed in Lyrical Ballads (1798): 'Alone on a wide wide sea'. There immensity is desolating; here it is liberating. 'Many-steepled tract' (printed 'track' in 1800) evokes the church towers of the Somerset parishes seen from the hills; the sea is the Bristol Channel.

title: My gentle-hearted Charles
short: Charles Lamb (1775-1834), Coleridge's schoolfellow at Christ's Hospital, then a clerk at the East India House in London.
body: The epithet 'gentle-hearted' recurs three times (ll. 29, 70, 77) and annoyed its subject. In August 1800, after the poem appeared in print, Lamb begged Coleridge not to make him ridiculous 'by terming me gentle-hearted in print', since 'gentle' 'almost always means poor-spirited'. Late in life Coleridge wrote beside the poem in his 1834 Poetical Works that Charles and Mary Lamb were 'dear to my heart'. Addressing a named friend is a defining device of the conversation poems: the poem is meant to be overheard by Lamb as well as read by us.

title: In the great City pent
short: Echoes Milton's simile of 'one who long in populous City pent' escaping into the fields (Paradise Lost 9.445).
body: Lamb, a London clerk, has 'pined / And hungered after Nature, many a year'. The phrase recalls Paradise Lost IX.445-51, where Satan, seeing Eve in the garden, is compared to one 'long in populous City pent' who goes out on a summer morning to breathe the air of the countryside. Coleridge borrows the townsman, not the menace, but the allusion gives Lamb's day in the hills the quality of an escape from confinement that matches Coleridge's own 'prison'. 'Frost at Midnight' (1798) uses the same word of Coleridge's London schooldays: 'pent 'mid cloisters dim'.

title: strange calamity
short: A veiled reference to September 1796, when Lamb's sister Mary, in a fit of madness, stabbed their mother to death.
body: In September 1796 Mary Lamb, suffering a mental breakdown, killed their mother with a knife. Charles, then twenty-one, undertook to be her guardian so that she would not be confined permanently to an asylum, and he looked after her for the rest of his life. Coleridge's 'through evil and pain / And strange calamity' alludes to this discreetly; the letter to Southey read 'sad yet bowed soul' where the printed text has 'sad yet patient soul'. Knowing the event gives weight to the wish that Lamb may stand 'Struck with deep joy' on the hill.

title: the sunset invocation
short: A rapturous run of imperatives: Coleridge bids sun, heath-flowers, clouds, groves and ocean intensify their colours for Lamb.
body: Here the absent poet behaves almost like a celebrant, calling on the landscape: 'slowly sink', 'Shine', 'richlier burn', 'Live', 'kindle'. The verbs are those of fire and light, and the scene rises to a sunset that will leave Lamb 'Silent with swimming sense'. The rhetoric recalls the psalms' summons to sun, moon and all creation to praise God (Psalm 148). It is the climax of the imagined journey, after which (l. 45) the mind returns to the bower.

title: Less gross than bodily ... veil the Almighty Spirit
short: The landscape seems almost immaterial, its colours both hiding and revealing God; Coleridge told Southey 'I am a Berkleyan'.
body: In the letter to Southey the passage read 'a living thing / That acts upon the mind, and with such hues / As clothe th' Almighty Spirit', with the note 'You remember I am a Berkleyan'. George Berkeley argued that material things exist only in being perceived and that nature is a language in which God speaks to us; 'Frost at Midnight' calls nature 'that eternal language, which thy God / Utters'. The change from 'clothe' to 'veil' (made in the errata of Sibylline Leaves) turns the colours into a covering that hides God while signalling his presence. Readers differ on how pantheistic the passage is: the revised wording keeps God more clearly distinct from the landscape.

title: the turn back to the bower
short: The poem's turn: sympathy with the walkers yields a sudden delight, and attention returns to the bower itself.
body: The conversation poems commonly follow an out-and-back pattern, from a present scene through memory or imagination and back to the scene with new understanding. M. H. Abrams made this the model of what he called the 'greater Romantic lyric', with this poem, 'Frost at Midnight' and 'Tintern Abbey' as examples. Here delight arrives 'As I myself were there', and with it Coleridge notices what he had overlooked: transparent lime leaves, shadows of leaf and stem, the walnut tree, the ivy. The label 'conversation poem' comes from Coleridge's subtitle for 'The Nightingale' (Lyrical Ballads, 1798).

sources.cite: M. H. Abrams, 'Structure and Style in the Greater Romantic Lyric' (1965), in From Sensibility to Romanticism, ed. F. W. Hilles and H. Bloom

title: the ivy that usurps the elms
short: Ivy smothering the elms, its dark mass catching the last light so that the elms' branches gleam in the twilight.
body: 'Usurps' is a political verb: the ivy has taken over the trees it climbs. Yet the effect is not sinister. The ivy's 'blackest mass' makes the elms' dark branches look lighter by contrast 'Through the late twilight'. The passage is one of several in which Coleridge records exact effects of light (dappling, transparency, gleam), the kind of observation found in his notebooks; critics such as Rosemary Ashton see the poem perfecting the plain, observant style begun in 'The Eolian Harp'.

title: humble-bee
short: The bumble-bee, still singing in the bean-flowers at dusk after bat and swallow have fallen silent.
body: 'Humble-bee' is the older English name of the bumble-bee (OED), from its humming. With the bat wheeling 'silent' and no swallow twittering, the bee's sound is the last sign of life in the garden, and it leads straight to the moral 'Henceforth I shall know'. Some readers take the solitary bee as a figure for the poet, alone but still singing.

title: the lesson of the bower
short: Coleridge draws the moral: no place is too narrow for Nature to engage the senses, and loss can enlarge sympathy.
body: 'Henceforth I shall know' announces knowledge the poem has earned. The confidence that 'Nature ne'er deserts the wise and pure' anticipates Wordsworth's 'Nature never did betray / The heart that loved her' in 'Tintern Abbey' (1798), written a year later within the same friendship. The second lesson, that it is sometimes well 'to be bereft of promised good' in order to 'contemplate / With lively joy the joys we cannot share', makes the poem an exercise in disinterested sympathy. The stops in 'but. may' (l. 64) and 'keep the heart.' (l. 65) in this text look like misprints; the sense runs on: keep the heart awake to Love and Beauty.

title: the last rook
short: A rook flying home across the setting sun links the poet in the bower with Lamb on the hill, and Coleridge 'blest it'.
body: Coleridge imagines that the rook he sees crossing the sunset is the same bird Lamb sees, so a single creature joins the separated friends in one act of perception. The blessing recalls the turning point of the Ancient Mariner, written in the same months, where the Mariner blesses the water-snakes 'unaware'. 'The mighty orb's dilated glory' is the setting sun, apparently enlarged near the horizon; '(Now a dim speck, now vanishing in light)' records the bird disappearing into the glare.

title: creeking
short: The creaking of the rook's wing-feathers; Coleridge later cited William Bartram's similar observation of the crane.
body: 'Creeking' is an old spelling of 'creaking' (OED). In a footnote Coleridge says that some months after writing the line he was pleased to find that William Bartram, in his Travels through North and South Carolina (1791), had noticed the same thing in the savanna crane, whose quill-feathers creak 'as the joints or working of a vessel in a tempestuous sea'. Bartram's Travels was a favourite book of Coleridge and Wordsworth in these years. The point is that even this harsh sound 'had a charm' for Lamb.

title: No sound is dissonant
short: The closing line: for Lamb every sound that signals life is harmonious, a version of Coleridge's idea of the 'one Life' in nature.
body: The poem ends not on the poet but on his friend, crediting Lamb with the generous perception the poem has been learning. 'Dissonant' is a musical term, and the line resolves the harsh 'creeking' into harmony. The idea that all things share one life appears in 'The Eolian Harp', whose lines on 'the one Life within us and abroad' were added in 1817. The final return to the addressee and to the evening scene is the conversation poem's characteristic close, with the speaker's mind changed since the start. Lamb himself disliked being praised in these terms; see the note on 'gentle-hearted'.
